title: Structures and pointers; arrow member access
learningObjectives: Declare a pointer to a structure type.
Use -> to access a member through a structure pointer.
Explain the equivalence of pointer->member and (*pointer).member.
Check pointer validity and object lifetime before member access.
Use pointer parameters to update caller-owned structure objects.

understand.concept: A pointer to a structure stores the address of a structure object. The arrow operator selects a member through that pointer; `p->member` is equivalent to `(*p).member`. The pointer must designate a live, correctly aligned structure object before member access. A non-null pointer alone does not prove validity.
understand.whyItMatters: Pointers avoid copying large structures and allow functions to update caller-owned records, but invalid or null pointers must not be dereferenced.
understand.analogy: Treat the operation as a clearly specified contract between the program and its data.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's type, lifetime, I/O and object representation rules.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Declare a structure pointer

If `struct Point` is a structure type, `struct Point *p` declares a pointer to such an object. Initialize it with the address of a live compatible object or a valid allocation.

## 2. Use the arrow operator

`p->x` accesses member x through p. It is equivalent to `(*p).x`; parentheses are needed because the dot operator binds more tightly than unary *.

## 3. Update through a pointer

A function can receive a structure pointer and modify members of the caller-owned object. The pointer argument itself is passed by value, but it designates the same object.

## 4. Validate before access

Check whether NULL is permitted and reject it before using ->. Also ensure the object is still alive and the pointer designates the correct type.

## 5. Ownership and lifetime

Document whether the function borrows the structure or owns allocated storage. Do not retain a pointer beyond the structure object's lifetime.

options: Yes, by assigning to members through the pointer
No, C copies the entire object every time

questions.answer: Yes, by assigning to members through the pointer
questions.explanation: The copied pointer value still designates the caller's structure object.
